newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco foes win tax round but next step uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco foes win tax round but next step uncertain.

text.p: Anti-smoking groups Tuesday welcomed a cigarette tax increase but said it does not necessarily presage more blows to tobacco when Congress takes up the proposed nationwide lawsuit settlement package later this year.

Congress and the White House agreed on a tax and spending plan late Monday that included a phased-in cigarette tax increase that would help finance children's health care. The tax would rise $0.10 a pack in the year 2000 and then go up another $0.05 in the year 2002.

Although that is far short of the $2 per pack increase that many public health groups say is needed to dissuade teenagers from starting to smoke, it is bigger than past increases. The last time the cigarette tax went up, in January 1993, it rose $0.04 to the present $0.24 a pack level.
"Fifteen cents is not going to be a disincentive to stop teens from smoking," said Judy Sopenski, director of a group known as Stop Teenage Smoking Now.
"But at least the tax shows (the tobacco industry) is not sacred and untouchable anymore and that in itself is valuable," she added.
"Every little bit helps and it's certainly better than Congress has done in ages," said Kathleen Scheg of Action on Smoking and Health.

But public health activists said the tax by no means guarantees clear sailing for new anti-tobacco initiatives. Pressed by lawsuits and accompanying disclosures about its health, safety and marketing record, the industry is on the defensive. But it also has a decades-long record of thwarting federal efforts to tax and regulate it.
Just last week, two other anti-tobacco initiatives failed in both houses of Congress.

One would have cut subsidized crop insurance for tobacco growers and the other would have given the U.S. Food and Drug Administration the $34 million it requested to enforce new rules against teen smoking.

"It's mixed signals," said David Shields, of the California-based Americans for NonSmokers Rights. "The FDA funding was certainly significant. The tax may represent a fairly significant increase but it's not going to hurt the tobacco industry."

Wrapped within a far larger bipartisan tax and spending package, the tobacco tax was conceived as a politically palatable way to pay for health care for uninsured children of the working poor. The Senate wanted a $0.20 tax hike, but it was scaled back in a compromise with the House.

"It's motherhood and apple pie," said Scheg. "You are taxing a destructive addictive drug to pay for children who don't have medical care. The only way someone could be against that is if they really have some allegiance to the tobacco industry."
The tobacco tax increase was not explicitly linked to the broader proposal to have the industry pay $368 billion to settle lawsuits brought against it by 40 states.

Congress is expected to take that plan up later this year. But with its complex provisions that have repercussions on the nation's liability laws, public health programs and government regulatory authority, it will be a far more complicated measure than the tax.
